items_missed: No real agenda statement. The opener was 'to see if you had a few minutes to discuss some of the details about your move and kind of see where I can get going from there' — a permission ask with no roadmap and no timeframe. Missing the two-part frame ('I'll gather some details, then walk you through pricing — about 10-15 minutes').

Never checked availability for the move date. He knew the date from the form ('I know like you were looking for the 9th of September, so it was kind of a short notice') and still hedged at the close with 'as long as we do have that availability' — he asked her to secure a spot he never confirmed existed, on a four-day-out move.

Never asked home size — the customer had to correct his own assumption. He said 'a few items like not a full apartment move kind of situation' and she came back with 'No, it's actually a two bedroom apartment.' The entire item list came from her volunteering it, not from probing.

Stairs and floors never asked at either end. This is an apartment origin and the transcript is explicit that the daughter uses a wheelchair — the single most load-time-relevant question on the call was never asked.
Access concerns never asked — no elevator, parking, gate, or truck-access question at an apartment complex, and nothing about access at the Lake Jackson house.

Packing was raised by the customer and dropped by the rep. She said 'let me see if I can find out if there are people who would pack up or stuff and bring it down here' — a direct buying signal for packing services. It was never acknowledged, never priced, and never factored into the hours.
Box count never asked despite 'she has boxes of stuff close computer personal stuff.'

No moving-stressor question, and no acknowledgment of the stressors she volunteered unprompted: 'my husband is about to be 75 I'm 69', 'I have a bad back so I don't know if I can help her', 'she has a wheelchair', and a daughter separating from a roommate. Every one drew 'For sure' or 'Sweet' and nothing else.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener. 'Straightforward simple. Shouldn't be that big of a deal' was said about the job, not the pricing structure.

No what's-included list at all — gas, truck, taxes, insurance, wrap, pads, bands, tools were never named. The only inclusion framing was the customer having to ask for it herself: 'is what you're quoting me including you helping her move that stuff out and putting it into the truck.'

Disassembly / reassembly never mentioned, even though she handed him the opening: 'one of them is glass on the top it comes apart.' A glass-top desk that needs breaking down and rebuilding is billable time he never explained or claimed as an included service.
No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. Glass furniture and computers on a three-and-a-half-hour highway run to a price-shopping customer, and the $2,000 coverage never came up.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned.

No full 'no hidden fees' pitch. He covered no deposit and no reschedule fee ('we don't require any fees, if we do need a skew around... no additional fee for that') but never the credit-card / transportation / fuel-surcharge / assembly-fee list — which matters more than usual here because he was simultaneously disclosing an $1,126 travel charge.

Clock-start never explained — no 'the clock starts on-site when the crew opens the contract.' 'You do only pay for the time that gets used on the day' is a billing reassurance, not a clock-start rule.

Estimate built on an unverified basis. The $2,374 total resolves arithmetically (6.5 hrs x $192 + $1,126), but the 6.5 hours is 3.5 hours of drive plus the 2.5-hour minimum, leaving effectively no labor time beyond the minimum for a partial two-bedroom load, a wheelchair, a glass desk to break down, and an unknown number of stairs at an apartment. Nothing in the probe supports that number.
No typical time range for the job — a single point estimate ('6.5 hours of work on the day give or take'), not a low-to-high range, and no reference to what moves like this usually run.

Move classification left ambiguous. He framed a San Antonio to Lake Jackson move (roughly 200 miles) as 'like if this is like a local move' and priced it on the local hourly plus a travel charge. Whether that is correct policy or not, the customer was never told which product she was being quoted.
Variables never explained: stairs/elevator, specialty items (the glass-top desk, the wheelchair), walk distance at the apartment, and packing time — all applicable, none covered.

Save Your Ass had the concept but none of the content. No consolidation examples (toys, loose drawer items, photos off walls) and no 'take a carload' tip — despite her literally proposing it herself: 'I thought about trying to get all this done with my, our two SUVs.' That was a free layup for 'anything small that fits in the SUV, take it — every box you move is time off the bill.'

Email contents never described — no BOLDED-details-at-the-top framing and no 'reply with any corrections so I know we have it right.' The closest line, 'if you have any other questions or updates for the move,' invites questions but never asks her to verify the details.
Customer's name used once, at the open, and mangled: 'calling for a Delo.' Never used again in a 7.7-minute call. Well short of the 3+ standard.
Effective insurance explanation missing entirely — neither No Worries nor the 60 cents per pound baseline.

Delivery was fragmented in a way that hurt the most important 30 seconds of the call. 'Sweet and sorry I kind of going over the hourly wait for two movers will be $192 an hour' — he self-corrected mid-pricing, then stacked $96, $192, $1,126, 6.5 hours and $2,374 in one breath to a 69-year-old customer with no pause to confirm she had the numbers down.
top_strength: Lukas ran a fast, confident, well-organized outbound callback and gave a price-shopping customer exactly what she called for, which she said out loud twice: 'that is exactly what I needed to know. It's a good starting point for me' and 'I appreciate you getting right back to me.' The address verification was genuinely sharp — he read both ends back off the form, 'the address that we have for currently at is gonna be the 18130 tele ridge, correct? And it looks like we're moving out to Houston but towards Houston over to the 210 Chestnut Street over in Lake Jackson, correct?', caught her correction to 212 and owned it cleanly ('212. Okay, gotcha my bad on that'). He then closed better than most: he volunteered no deposit and no reschedule fee before being asked ('we don't require any deposit to get you on the schedule as well just to kind of put that on the radar'), answered her holiday-hours question with real specifics ('We're open Monday, we're even open tomorrow if need be'), made a direct and well-framed booking attempt that respected where she actually was in her process ('would you like to secure the spot while you're looking around... just in case, or just wanna get the quote hold onto it and kind of compare quotes'), and verified her email address letter by letter before promising delivery in minutes. Budget framing was consistent and on-brand throughout: 'you do only pay for the time that gets used' and 'if it takes less time... by all means, we'll just pay less at the end of the day.'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix is the probe, because on this call the probe is the estimate. Lukas quoted 6.5 hours and $2,374 without ever asking whether the daughter's apartment is on the second floor, how far the walk to the truck is, how many boxes there are, or whether the glass-top desk needs breaking down — and he quoted it to a customer who had already told him she uses a wheelchair and that the desk 'comes apart.' Before the price he needed to say: 'Delia, two quick things so I get your hours right — is her apartment upstairs or ground floor, and how far is the walk from her door to where the truck can park? And you mentioned the glass-top desk comes apart — we'll break that down and rebuild it at the house, that's included, I just want to build the time in.' Those three answers are the difference between a quote that holds and a bad move-day surprise on a job that is already an estimate-accuracy risk. Second priority: she asked for packing and he never answered. 'Let me see if I can find out if there are people who would pack up our stuff' is a buying signal for a higher-ticket service, and the line was 'We absolutely pack — it's the same $96 per mover per hour plus materials, and for a load this size it usually adds an hour or two. Want me to quote it both ways so you can see the difference?' That is revenue left on the table and an accuracy gap at the same time. Third: three differentiators went unsaid on the call where they mattered most. No Worries in particular was gift-wrapped — glass furniture and computers going 200 miles down the highway to a customer comparing bids on price alone. 'Everything gets wrapped and padded, and you're covered by our No Worries Damage Coverage — up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace, or reimburse anything we damage. That's included, not an add-on.' Pair that with Meet Your Mover and the On-Time Guarantee and she has three reasons to pick Einstein that no competitor's cheaper hourly rate answers. Fourth, and this is the human one: she told him she is 69, her husband is nearly 75, she has a bad back, and her daughter is in a wheelchair after a hard living situation. Every disclosure got 'For sure' or 'Sweet.' One sentence would have changed the whole call — 'That sounds like a lot to carry on your own, and honestly that's exactly what we're for — you don't need to lift a thing, our guys will handle all of it.' She is buying relief, not hours. Finally, slow the pricing recap down and separate it into pieces with a check after each: rate, then travel charge, then hours, then total, then 'does that all line up with what you were expecting?' Stacking five numbers into one self-corrected sentence is how a price-shopper writes down the wrong figure and compares it against a competitor.
phone_presence_notes: Upbeat and easy to talk to on the surface, and the customer left the call happy ('Thank you so much'), but the warmth was filler rather than connection — 'Sweet,' 'For sure' and 'by all means' repeated throughout while significant personal disclosures about her age, her back, and her daughter's wheelchair drew no empathy at all, and her name was used once and mispronounced.
audio_review_reason: Two reasons. First, the transcript is noticeably garbled in spots ('calling for a Delo,' 'toll worlds,' 'pell out a little bit early,' 'if we do need a skew around,' 'an idea desk'), so it is unclear how much is transcription error versus rushed speech. Second, the pricing recap is the load-bearing moment of the call and it reads as a self-corrected run-on ('Sweet and sorry I kind of going over the hourly wait for two movers will be $192 an hour'); audio is needed to judge whether the $1,126 travel charge and $2,374 total were actually delivered clearly enough for the customer to write down, and whether the flat responses to her personal disclosures sounded dismissive or merely brisk.
